792.title: Subha and the stranger
792.hook: a man blocks Subha's path in a mango grove, praising her eyes; she shows him what an eye is (Therigatha, Subha)
792.howItsDone: Contemplating the parts of the body is a traditional Buddhist practice for loosening desire, and teachers sometimes tell Subha's story to show that practice used as a clear refusal.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sacca: Ambapali walked her own body, then and now, and found the truth-speaker's word holds. Your line was so it was, so it is. Today, another nun, and a man who won't let her pass.

A path through a mango grove, the one known as Jivaka's. A nun named Subha is walking it. A man steps into her way and stays there. What wrong have I done you, she asks, that you stand in my path? It isn't fitting for a man to touch a woman who has gone forth. He doesn't step aside. He starts talking instead: about her youth, about the forest in flower, and more than anything, about her eyes.
screen: `JIVAKA'S MANGO GROVE.` → `A MAN BLOCKS THE PATH.` → `WHAT WRONG HAVE I DONE YOU?`

segments.voice: First, his pitch. He offers her a life of comfort: fine cloth, ornaments, a house, the grove in bloom and full of birdsong. Give up the robe, he says. And he keeps returning to her eyes, like a doe's, he says; nothing is dearer to him. Second, her answer. Subha takes his praise apart. What is this body you're so taken with? What is an eye? A little ball set in a hollow, she says, with a bubble in the middle and tears around it. She compares a body to a painted puppet. She has seen through what he's selling. Third, the act. Then the poem does something startling. She plucks out her eye and holds it out to him: here, take it. His desire vanishes on the spot. He asks her forgiveness, wishes her well, and lets her go. Fourth, the ending. Subha goes on to the Buddha, and the poem says that when she saw him, her eye was restored as it had been. What to make of a story like this? Some readers hear renunciation pushed to its limit. Others hear a woman refusing to be reduced to a part of her body: he wanted the eye, so she showed him what an eye is. The poem tells it once, as her answer, not as a thing anyone is asked to repeat. And its first line still stands on its own: she names the wrong plainly, before anything else happens.

segments.voice: Bring to mind one unwanted pull, a sales pitch, a tug from your phone, a habit of saying yes, and hear Subha's first question: what wrong have I done, that you stand in my path? Let a no form, plain and unhurried. If someone is truly blocking your path the way the man in the grove did, that calls for more than a breath: tell someone you trust.
Cakkhu. The eye: the word behind Subha's question to a stranger who praised her eyes on a forest path, what is an eye? Today's word.
Your line: what is an eye. Her first words named the wrong, plainly. See you tomorrow.

793.title: Punnika's question
793.hook: a water-carrier asks a brahmin: if bathing washed away evil, wouldn't the fish and frogs be saints? (Therigatha, Punnika)
793.howItsDone: Some Buddhist teachers read Punnika's verses as a teaching that purity comes from conduct and intention, and tell of a water-carrier whose plain question changed a priest's life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, cakkhu: Subha asked a man who praised her eyes, what is an eye? Your line was what is an eye. Today, another woman with a question, at a river.

Why would anyone stand in a river in the cold if they didn't have to? Punnika has to. She carries water for a household, and in her verses she says she goes down into the water in the cold, afraid of her mistresses' punishment. At the river she finds a brahmin, a priest, standing in the water, shivering. She's there because she has to be. Why is he? So she asks him.
screen: `A WATER-CARRIER IN THE COLD.` → `A BRAHMIN, SHIVERING.` → `WHY ARE YOU HERE?`

segments.voice: First, her question. Brahmin, what are you afraid of, she asks, that you go down into the water with your limbs shaking in the cold? She knows what drives her. She wonders what drives him. Second, his answer. He's doing good to undo evil, he says: whoever has done wrong, young or old, is freed of it by bathing. Third, the frogs. Who told you that, she asks, someone who didn't know, telling someone else who didn't? If water washed away wrongdoing, then the frogs and the turtles, the water snakes and the crocodiles would all go to heaven. And if the river carried off your wrongs, it would carry off your good deeds too, and leave you with nothing. Fourth, what she offers instead. If you fear suffering, she says, don't do harmful things, openly or in secret. And she adds a kindness: don't let your body suffer in the cold. The brahmin is moved. He thanks her for turning him from the wrong road and takes refuge, and the poem ends with him saying that now he is truly washed. The washing still matters; it has moved from the skin to the deeds. This poem is one voice in an old conversation, told from inside the Buddha's community; in the Majjhima the Buddha makes a similar point about bathing in sacred rivers. Hindus who bathe in holy rivers today speak for themselves about what that bathing means, and this poem doesn't speak for them.

Ask it Punnika's question, plainly: what is this for? You don't need to stop doing it, and sometimes the answer makes it richer; just ask, and listen for what comes back.

794.title: Isidasi's story
794.hook: three husbands sent her back; she tells the long tale behind it (Therigatha, Isidasi)
794.howItsDone: Isidasi's poem is read in Buddhist communities as a teaching on kamma across lives, and modern readers also discuss it as an account of a woman's marriages told in her own voice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Punnika asked a shivering brahmin why he bathed. Your line was the frogs would be saints. Today, a nun who is asked why, and answers at length.

Two nuns sit together after the alms round, in the city of Pataliputta. One of them, Bodhi, asks the other a question that's half compliment and half puzzle. You're still young, and lovely, she says. What did you see that made you leave the world? The other nun is Isidasi. She doesn't answer with a slogan. She tells the whole story, and it's long, and it doesn't flatter anyone, not even herself.
screen: `TWO NUNS AFTER THE ALMS ROUND.` → `WHY DID YOU LEAVE THE WORLD?` → `SHE TELLS EVERYTHING.`

segments.voice: First, the faithful wife. Isidasi says she was married into a merchant family in Saketa, and did all a daughter-in-law was expected to do. She bowed to her in-laws morning and evening, cooked, cleaned, served her husband with her own hands. And still he came to hate her. When his parents asked what she had done, she told them: nothing. I've done no wrong. They sent her home to her father. Second, again and again. Her father gave her to a second husband, who sent her back too. Then he invited a wandering beggar to stay as his son-in-law. Before long the man asked for his begging bowl and robe back, and left. Three times, and no one could name a fault. So, with her father's blessing, she went forth. Third, the longer story. Here the poem turns. Isidasi says she can now see her past lives: once a goldsmith who went after other men's wives, then long suffering, then births as animals, then hard human lives. In her telling, being sent away in this life was that old deed ripening. Fourth, how to hear it. Some readers find this ending hard, because it can sound like blaming a woman for being rejected. But notice what the poem insists on first: in this life she did nothing wrong. The past-life story is her searching out the whole shape of what happened, further back than one life, and then setting it down. She ends the poem free of all of it.

795.title: Sumedha refuses
795.hook: a princess refuses marriage to a king, cuts her hair and argues her way to the order (Therigatha, Sumedha)
795.howItsDone: In Buddhist traditions, going forth as a nun or monk is a decision families take seriously, and the Therigatha's stories of women who argued for it, like Sumedha's, are read as examples of resolve.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Isidasi told Bodhi the whole story, back through other lives. Your line was the whole story. Today, a princess who says no to a king.

A sword, used for a haircut. Sumedha is a king's daughter in the city of Mantavati, and she has been promised in marriage to another king, Anikaratta. She has heard the nuns teach, and she wants to go forth. Her parents want the wedding. The poem that tells her story is long, and much of it is talk: argument after argument from a young woman who will not be talked out of what she has chosen.
screen: `A PRINCESS, PROMISED TO A KING.` → `SHE WANTS TO GO FORTH.` → `ARGUMENT AFTER ARGUMENT.`

segments.voice: First, the argument at home. Sumedha tells her parents she wants to go forth, and they weep and plead: a royal marriage is waiting for her. She answers them with the teaching. Life is short, she says, and pleasures don't last. She reaches for pictures the Buddha's discourses use for sense pleasures: a dream that ends on waking, goods that are only borrowed. She isn't sulking. She's making a case. Second, the hair. When the pleading doesn't stop, she cuts off her own hair with a sword, shuts the palace doors, and sits down. The poem says she entered the first stage of meditative absorption, right there. Third, the king. Anikaratta arrives, dressed for a wedding, with gold and jewels, and offers her wealth and every pleasure a kingdom has. She doesn't run, and she doesn't give in. She answers him as patiently as she argued with her parents. Fourth, the result. In the poem, the king ends up asking her father to let her go forth. She wins not by slipping away in the night, but by making her case to every person standing in the doorway, until there is no one left to persuade. Her refusal is a no to the wedding, and a yes to something she can explain.

If the decision still stands, let yourself stand with it, calmly, for these breaths; if it doesn't, that's worth knowing too.

796.title: Sona's strength
796.hook: the mother of ten who ordained late: effort in old age (Therigatha, Sona)
796.howItsDone: In Buddhist communities, people sometimes ordain or take up serious practice late in life, and Sona's verses are remembered as a sign that effort on the path does not depend on youth.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sumedha argued until even the king asked that she be let go. Your line was she argued her way in. Today, a nun who came late, and the strength she found.

Shame on you, wretched old age. That's how Sona's song ends, and it reads almost like a dare. The path has met her before, in the commentary's story of a late start and a pot of bath water. Today stays with her own verses. She bore ten sons, she says, and by the time she went to a nun to hear the teaching, she was weak and old. No royal refusal, no dramatic escape. A tired body, and a decision.
screen: `SHAME ON YOU, OLD AGE.` → `TODAY, HER OWN VERSES.` → `WEAK AND OLD, SHE GOES.`

segments.voice: First, where she started. Having borne ten sons from this body, she says, weak and old, I went to a nun. She doesn't dress it up. Her strength was gone before her practice began. Second, what she heard. The nun taught her the basics: the heaps that make up a person, the senses, the elements. Sona heard it, cut off her hair, and went forth. Nothing in her verses says she waited to feel stronger first. Third, what she found. While she trained, she says, the divine eye was made clear, and she came to know her former lives. Her mind became steady and one-pointed. She was freed, clinging to nothing, at peace. The heaps that make up a person, she says, are fully known, and stand now cut off at the root. Fourth, the dare. Then she turns to old age itself. Shame on you, she says, wretched old age; there's no more coming back. Old age had taken her strength of body. It hadn't taken her effort. The strength in the title isn't muscle. In Sona's song it's the will to keep at it, and it didn't wait for her to be young.

797.title: The brothers' songs
797.hook: poems of the first monks: forests, rain, freedom
797.howItsDone: In Theravada communities, verses from the Theragatha are read and taught alongside the Therigatha, and teachers often draw on single poems from it as short reflections.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sona, who came to the order late and found her strength there. Your line was strength in old age. Today, the songs turn from the sisters to the brothers.

Rain on a thatched roof. A peacock calling somewhere in the trees. A man sitting alone in a forest, saying out loud that he is free. These aren't scenes from a novel. They're lines from poems that Buddhist tradition gives to the early monks themselves. The sisters' songs, the Therigatha, have a companion: a book of the brothers' songs. Today it opens, and today's word is its name.
screen: `RAIN ON A THATCHED ROOF.` → `THE SISTERS' BOOK HAS A COMPANION.` → `TODAY IT OPENS.`

segments.voice: First, the name. Theragatha. A thera is an elder, a senior monk, and a gatha is a verse: verses of the elders. Second, the voice. Each poem carries a monk's name, and tradition says the monk himself spoke it, often about the moment he was freed, or looking back on the road there. So these aren't sermons about the monks. They're his own words, in the first person: I went to the forest, I sat, I was set free. Third, what they sing about. Forests. Caves and rocky hills. Clouds and rain. Peacocks, elephants, cranes. And again and again, freedom: the work is done, the burden is down, there is nothing more to do. Some poems are a single verse. Some run on for pages, and in one of them a monk argues with his own mind. Fourth, how to read them. Some readers find them strangely close: a man in a hut, listening to the rain, and glad. Others notice how much they repeat, the same phrases closing poem after poem, almost like a chorus. Both are there: a shared chorus, and one person's afternoon of rain and peacocks. The brothers' book sits beside the sisters' among the short texts of the Pali canon. In the days ahead come some of these brothers by name: a monk with a dry roof, a man who swept away old flowers, a former bandit, an actor, the great disciples. Each one, in his own words.

When the mind wanders off, come back to that line the way you'd come back to the breath.

798.title: My hut is roofed
798.hook: Subhuti: my hut is roofed and snug; rain, god, if you like (Theragatha 1.1)
798.howItsDone: Forest monks in the Theravada tradition still live in small huts called kutis, and teachers often read Subhuti's short poem as a picture of a mind at ease whatever the weather.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Theragatha, the brothers' songs. Your line was his own words. Today, the poem that stands at the head of that book.

A roof, a mind, and a dare to the weather. A monk named Subhuti sits in a small hut, and what he says to the sky is the poem numbered first in the brothers' book. It isn't a plea for the rain to stop, or a complaint about the leaks. It's closer to an invitation: freedom, talking back to the weather.
screen: `A ROOF, A MIND, A DARE.` → `A MONK IN A SMALL HUT.` → `HE TALKS BACK TO THE SKY.`

segments.voice: First, the hut. Subhuti says his hut is roofed, pleasant, and sheltered from the wind. A small thing, done well. In the wet season, a good roof is the difference between sitting through the night and running for cover. Second, the mind. In the same breath he says his mind is well settled, and freed. Two shelters side by side, both finished. One keeps the water out. The other no longer lets the old storms in. Third, the dare. So rain, god, if you like, he says. The poem speaks to the rain as a god, the one who sends it, and Subhuti isn't asking that god for anything. Rain, or don't. He's covered either way. Fourth, why it's a fitting door into the book. The poem is tiny, but it holds the whole Theragatha in small: the weather, a man alone, and the quiet news that the work is done. Some readers hear a little swagger in it. Others hear relief, the voice of someone who used to dread the storm and doesn't anymore. The poem doesn't say which, and it doesn't need to. A dry roof isn't nothing. Neither is a settled mind. Put the two together and the sky can do what it likes.
screen: `A ROOF, SNUG AND OUT OF THE WIND.` · `A MIND, SETTLED AND FREED.` · `RAIN, GOD, IF YOU LIKE.` · `THE WHOLE BOOK IN A FEW LINES.` · then, large: `RAIN IF YOU LIKE.`

segments.voice: Sit snugly, as if it's raining, and if it is, listen to it; notice what's covering you right now, a chair at your back, a blanket on your knees, the walls around you. Then turn to the mind and see what leaks in, a worry, a plan, a noise from the next room, and let it drip without fixing the roof. If you like, say Subhuti's words quietly to whatever's coming: rain, if you like.
Kuti. A hut, the forest monk's small dwelling: the shelter in Subhuti's opening words in the Theragatha, a settled mind inside, so let it rain. Today's word.
Your line: rain if you like. The brothers' book opens with only a few lines, and a mind at ease in the rain. See you tomorrow.
